notes: Full TCC judgment on enforcement of construction adjudicator's decision.

enrichment.short_title: Enforcement of adjudicator's decision on defective marina gate design

statutes_considered.name: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: Dean and Dyball Construction claimed £315,390.14 from consulting engineer Kenneth Grubb Associates following an adjudicator's decision on a Watchet Marina tidal gate that failed to operate reliably.
The parties' contract incorporated ACE Conditions B(2), including clause B9.2 providing for CIC Model Adjudication Procedure adjudication.
Grubb resisted summary enforcement on grounds including s 107 'in writing', crystallised dispute, wrong question decided, error of law, and procedural unfairness from separate expert meetings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 24 summary judgment application to enforce an adjudicator's decision in the TCC.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment for the claimant; adjudicator's decision enforced with all objections rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Where a construction contract incorporating the ACE Conditions provides express adjudication under the CIC Model Adjudication Procedure, enforcement will not fail because of arguable s 107 issues, provided a crystallised liability dispute existed despite changing quantum, the adjudicator decided the referred dispute by applying the reasonable skill and care standard, and separate meetings with parties and experts did not breach natural justice where substance was circulated and no undisclosed material was relied on.
legal_issues: Whether the contract was a construction contract 'in writing' under s 107 HGCRA 1996
Whether a crystallised dispute existed when notice of adjudication was served
Whether the adjudicator decided the dispute referred or applied the wrong legal test
Whether separate adjudicator meetings with parties and experts were procedurally unfair

notes: Full Chancery judgment striking out long-running solicitor negligence claim as abuse.

enrichment.short_title: Perotti estate litigation against solicitors struck out as abuse
key_facts: Litigant in person Angelo Perotti sued solicitors and counsel retained briefly in 1993 over advice in long-running proceedings concerning Lorenzo Perotti's estate, including undisclosed Swiss funds.
Claims included failure to appeal Roger Kaye QC's orders, failure to plead absence of a charging clause, Nestle-type investment loss claims, and other causes said to be worth up to £2 million.
Identical issues had already been determined against Perotti in actions before Lloyd J, Lindsay J, Master Moncaster, and the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendants' applications to strike out for abuse and for summary judgment under CPR Part 24.
enrichment.outcome: Claim struck out as abuse of process; alternatively summary judgment for defendants with particulars of claim struck out.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant seeks to relitigate professional negligence claims against lawyers already adjudicated in other proceedings, the claim is an abuse under Bairstow unless manifest unfairness or disrepute to justice would result; a litigant in person who had years to raise Nestle investment and charging-clause points cannot revive them against later advisers, and conference notes showing adverse advice on those points defeat denial at a late stage.
legal_issues: Whether the claim is an abuse of process under Secretary of State for Trade and Industry v Bairstow
Whether Perotti's claims against these defendants have any real prospect of success
Whether Henderson v Henderson bars Nestle investment claims not raised in the main action
Whether conference notes showed clients were advised on charging clause and investment claims

notes: Short Divisional Court judgment dismissing habeas corpus after extradition committal.

enrichment.short_title: Habeas corpus refused after Czech extradition committal
key_facts: The applicant was committed at Bow Street Magistrates' Court on 29 January 2003 to await the Secretary of State's decision on a Czech Republic extradition request relating to shop and car theft and misuse of stolen cards.
He was granted conditional bail but lost contact with his solicitors from July 2003.
Habeas corpus grounds included dual criminality, alleged racist motivation, authentication defects, triviality, and bad faith.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court application for habeas corpus following extradition committal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; district judge's decision upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where every ground raised on habeas corpus was fully argued and rejected by the extradition magistrate, and nothing has since transpired to cast doubt on that decision, the Divisional Court will dismiss the application.
legal_issues: Whether dual criminality was satisfied for Czech requested offences
Whether extradition was sought on racist grounds against a Roma applicant
Whether the extradition request was duly authenticated
Whether habeas corpus can reopen fully determined extradition objections

notes: Full TCC judgment on validity of draft and late adjudicator decisions.

enrichment.short_title: Late adjudicator decision binding despite draft publication process

statutes_considered.name: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Adjudicator Anthony Barker issued a draft decision on 17 June 2002 inviting comments and a final decision on 25 June 2002 in a JCT dispute over extension-of-time claims on the Ely Central Area Redevelopment project.
Simons argued the draft was not a binding decision and the final decision was invalid because issued after the agreed 17 June deadline.
Clause 39A of the JCT building contract and the JCT Adjudication Agreement governed timing and termination of the adjudicator's appointment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 20 declaratory proceedings transferred to the TCC concerning validity of adjudication decisions and adjudicator fees.
enrichment.outcome: Draft decision held not a valid decision; final decision dated 25 June 2002 declared binding on the parties.
enrichment.ratio: A document marked as a draft and inviting unrestricted party comments is not a concluded adjudication decision; however, an adjudicator who misses the contractual deadline does not lose jurisdiction to issue a binding decision unless the adjudication agreement is jointly terminated or a fresh referral is made, so a late final decision remains enforceable as a procedural irregularity rather than a nullity.
legal_issues: Whether a draft adjudicator decision inviting comments is a valid 'decision'
Whether failure to decide by the agreed deadline deprives the adjudicator of jurisdiction
Whether late publication invalidates an adjudication decision under JCT clause 39A and the Scheme

notes: Full Chancery trial judgment on competing title to rugby club ground.

enrichment.short_title: Pre-emption exercised over moribund Bryant Homes sale contract
key_facts: Coventry Rugby Club's trustees granted Leander Bromley a five-year pre-emption over Barker Butts Lane ground in August 1996.
Bryant Homes contracted to buy the ground in April 1998 conditional on satisfactory planning and non-exercise of pre-emption; Leander did not accept within two months.
After the club was wound up in September 1998, liquidators sold the ground to Leander Hotels (later Butts Park Ventures) for £150,000 in April 2002 following valid pre-emption exercise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of competing claims to freehold title and registration priority.
enrichment.outcome: Butts Park's title upheld; Bryant's caution to be vacated and Bryant declared to have no subsisting interest.
enrichment.ratio: A conditional contract for sale does not 'dispose' of land so as to exhaust a pre-emption until completion; where pre-emption is later validly exercised, a prior conditional sale agreement whose condition precedent includes non-exercise of pre-emption can never become unconditional; and the court's equitable winding-up jurisdiction may appoint persons with liquidator-like powers to sell an unincorporated association's property.
legal_issues: Whether the Leander pre-emption agreement satisfied s 2 LP(MP)A 1989
Whether the Bryant agreement constituted a disposal exhausting pre-emption
Whether equitable winding-up could confer valid sale powers on liquidators
Whether Bryant's contract retained priority after pre-emption exercise

notes: Full admin court judgment on student visa application validity.

enrichment.short_title: Incomplete student visa form not a valid extension application
key_facts: Jamaican visitor admitted in December 2001 enrolled at Blackheath Bluecoat School and applied in May 2002 to extend stay as a student before initial leave expired in June 2002.
The form omitted answers on study progress, course type, monthly financial support, and three months' bank statements required by Section 7.
The Home Office later treated a deficient October 2002 form as the operative application and refused on substantive student-rule grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging refusal of leave to remain and absence of appeal rights.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; May application held invalid with no right of appeal.
enrichment.ratio: An application to vary leave must use the prescribed form completed as required and accompanied by specified documents; omissions as to Rule 57 institution type and financial evidence are not cured by partial enclosures, there is no doctrine of substantial compliance in immigration form requirements, and relief would be refused in discretion where the school was a maintained school outside Rule 57 in any event.
legal_issues: Whether the May 2002 application was valid under Immigration Rule 32
Whether substantial compliance can save an incomplete student application
Whether late Home Office correspondence created a valid application or appeal rights
Whether maintained-school attendance brought the claimant within any exception

notes: Court of Appeal refusal of permission to appeal s 69 arbitration decision.

enrichment.short_title: No appeal where TCC judge properly decided JCT certificate issues
key_facts: Wright & Fuller claimed about £75,000 under a JCT final certificate; the arbitrator decided preliminary issues on validity under clauses 30.8 and 30.9 in the contractor's favour.
On s 69 appeal Thornton J initially drafted answers favouring the employer, then revised after objection that he had exceeded jurisdiction by making new findings.
The applicant sought permission to appeal alleging procedural unfairness and excess of jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal a Technology and Construction Court decision under Arbitration Act 1996 s 69.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 69 appeal the judge may construe the contract and certificate using all material before the arbitrator and make any findings necessary to answer the defined questions of law, provided findings are not contrary to the arbitrator's; such conduct is not procedural unfairness akin to misconduct warranting intervention under section 69(8).
legal_issues: Whether a section 69 judge exceeds jurisdiction by making additional findings of fact
Whether the judge redefined the questions of law on appeal
Whether procedural unfairness under section 69(8) arises where new reasons were not argued at first instance

notes: Court of Appeal judgment on recovery of union-funded CFA success fees.

enrichment.short_title: Trade union CCFA success fee recoverable from defendant
key_facts: Claimant union member settled a road traffic personal injury claim for £2,349.67 plus reasonable costs but parties disputed a 20% success fee under a collective conditional fee agreement between the union and solicitors.
Defendant's insurers accepted liability for base costs but argued the success fee was not recoverable because the claimant incurred no personal liability under the indemnity principle.
Legal services were provided under a valid CCFA and a client care letter stated the union would indemnify the claimant for costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal in county court costs-only proceedings under Part 8.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 20% success fee held recoverable as part of reasonable costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant acquiesces in solicitors acting under a union CCFA and accepts liability for costs, he comes under an enforceable obligation to pay on the agreed conditional terms; that obligation arises from the CCFA regime rather than the stricter individual CFA Regulations, so the indemnity principle permits recovery of the success fee from the paying party.
legal_issues: Whether the indemnity principle bars recovery of union-funded success fees
Whether a litigant must enter an individual CFA complying with CFA Regulations to incur recoverable costs
Whether a valid CCFA creates personal liability despite third-party funding
Effect of section 58A(6) on the indemnity principle

notes: Full QB judgment rejecting contributory negligence in breakdown collision.

enrichment.short_title: No contributory negligence for broken-down car with hazards on
key_facts: Claimant's Metro broke down on the nearside lane of the A13 at Basildon in wet daylight conditions; hazard lights were on and the car was about one foot from the nearside white line.
Defendant admitted primary liability but alleged contributory negligence for driving when breakdown was foreseeable, parking position, and remaining in the vehicle.
Defendant saw the car 200-250 yards away but moved into the nearside lane and failed to see hazard lights until 50 yards away, colliding at about 45 mph.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on contributory negligence only in a running-down action where liability was admitted.
enrichment.outcome: All allegations of contributory negligence rejected.
enrichment.ratio: A stationary broken-down vehicle with flashing hazard warning lights visible from a considerable distance on a dual carriageway does not present a dangerous obstruction to motorists exercising ordinary care; a driver who moves into the partially blocked nearside lane and fails to see the hazards until too late cannot rely on the claimant's position or presence in the car where the collision resulted from highly negligent driving the claimant was not bound to anticipate.
legal_issues: Whether driving despite known mechanical problems was contributory negligence
Whether stopping one foot from the nearside edge rather than fully off the road was negligent
Whether sitting in a broken-down car on the carriageway was contributory negligence
Whether hazard lights made the obstruction non-dangerous to reasonably careful drivers

notes: Court of Appeal judgment on commoners' grazing and vehicle rights on golf course.

enrichment.short_title: Commoner may use vehicles to tend sheep but not bring feed
key_facts: Mr John, a registered commoner with sheep grazing rights on Vaynor Common, used part of a golf club's land where his hefted flock grazed.

The club complained he drove vehicles beyond hard tracks, damaged greens, and brought supplementary feed; Mr John counterclaimed that mowing fairways after expanding to 18 holes in 1994 interfered with grazing.
The county court declared he could not bring feed on and could drive only to remove sick animals or carcasses on existing tracks.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Merthyr Tydfil County Court declarations and injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; no right to bring feed affirmed; limited right to use vehicles for welfare/shepherding recognised but remitted for agreed order; counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A right of common pasture is limited to eating grass grown on the common and does not include bringing supplementary feed onto the land; however, tending sheep welfare is a necessary incident of pasturage and may prima facie be exercised by vehicle in modern conditions, subject to reasonableness and minimum interference with the landowner, while mowing fairways on a small part of a large common does not materially restrict grazing rights.
legal_issues: Whether bringing feed is ancillary to a right of grazing
Whether motor vehicles may be used for shepherding and welfare checks
When vehicle use is necessity versus convenience
Whether golf course expansion and mowing unreasonably interfered with grazing rights
